paragraphs: I did clinical clerkships from February to April at the University of Freiburg in southwestern Germany. In this overseas exchange program, which at three months was the longest, I would like to describe below what I experienced and learned in "the city with the most hours of sunshine in Germany."

The official name of the city I went to is Freiburg im Breisgau. In fact, there are several cities named Freiburg in Europe. In Germany, which has an image of industrial cities, the town of Freiburg, located around the Schwarzwald (Black Forest), is a charming town paved with cobblestones that retains traces of the Middle Ages while having abundant nature. The population is 230,000, about one tenth of Nagoya, of whom 30,000 are students. It was a typical university town. The University of Freiburg, founded in 1457, is the second university in the Habsburg Empire after the Medical University of Vienna. Of course it is also one of the oldest universities in Germany. The university hospital has 1,600 beds compared with Nagoya University Hospital's 1,080, and is one of the largest hospitals in Germany.

Because I aspire to surgical fields, the University of Freiburg medical school, which accepts students only in surgical departments, was a perfect destination. (As a rule there is a language standard for exchange students, but there is none for Nagoya University students. For those who want to do clerkships in internal medicine, level B2 or B1 is required.) I asked for clerkships in gastrointestinal surgery, urology, orthopedics and so on, and submitted the documents at the end of the summer of my fifth year. Notice of acceptance came quickly, but the notice that coordination with the departments had been completed finally came in December. Moreover, the result of the coordination was February: forensic medicine, March: infection control, April: otorhinolaryngology. Because of misunderstandings on their side and so on, I was to start differently from what I had expected, but following the advice of Dr. 長谷川 of the International Collaboration Office, I went to Europe having resolved to negotiate directly with my preferred departments on site and have it rearranged. After arriving, I exchanged many emails with the doctors and secretaries of my preferred departments. I continued negotiating while fighting homesickness and loneliness. In the end the negotiation succeeded, and I was able to do a very satisfying clerkship in my own preferred departments.

The clerkship schedule became February: forensic medicine, March: infection control (2 weeks) and neurosurgery (3 weeks), April: general surgery. In forensic medicine I observed and took part in forensic autopsies. The kidneys and liver are apparently easy, and in the latter half of the clerkship I was sometimes entrusted with them. Besides seeing in front of my eyes what I had learned in forensic medicine lectures, it was impressive to see a burned body and to learn about cooperation with the police. In infection control, I studied hygiene management of the hospital's air conditioning and water quality, nosocomial infection, tracing of transmission routes, and instructions for isolation. Unlike Nagoya University Hospital, Freiburg University Hospital has facilities separated by department and has many buildings, so I learned the importance of grasping the problems of each one and ensuring and raising the quality of care. Also, when I said I aspired to surgery, they taught me about the hygiene of surgical instruments, and I also visited the washing facility. Forensic medicine and infection control are parts one cannot see in the clinical clerkships in Japan, so I could have a valuable experience. When I rotated through neurosurgery, I took part in the rounds and conference every day from 7 o'clock and observed operations during the day. The neurosurgery doctors gave a lecture on diseases that must not be missed in the emergency department, and I did ward work, and I was able to spend a meaningful three weeks. In general surgery as well I spent time from 7 in the morning mixed in with the local sixth-year students. Every day I took part in the surgical field as an assistant, and in ward work I did drain removal, skin suturing and blood draws. The local sixth-year students are called PJ (Praktisches Jahr: Practical Year), and I felt their position is close to that of residents in Japan. I was impressed by the excellence of the local students, and it led to a boost in my own motivation. Above all, I savored the joy of being able to do surgical clerkships because I had taken a step forward myself and negotiated with the departments and the administration.

The University of Freiburg did not provide a dormitory. I searched for and booked places with good conditions through Airbnb and the like myself and spent the three months. My lodging was the type where one lives with a host family, and fortunately the hosts were kind and took good care of me. Prices were not so different from Japan except for eating out, and the weather was worthy of "the city with the most hours of sunshine in Germany," with sunny scenes unlike winter in Germany, and it was a livable environment. Outside the clerkships, on weekdays I went drinking with local students at German restaurants and student bars and studied together in the library. On weekends I enjoyed traveling in Europe with friends I made there and Nagoya University students who were studying abroad in other cities. I was able to have many experiences I could not have had in Japan, and they became brilliant memories.

What I realized through this overseas exchange program is the vastness of the world and my own smallness. I had been living in a comfortable environment surrounded by familiar faces, but I witnessed values change by showing courage and initiative. I think it was because I faced it with a mindset of experiencing everything with all my might that it led to success. It was an irreplaceable experience in which I grew many times over as a person, acquiring breadth of perspective and initiative, besides growth in study and language. Finally, I would like to thank everyone who supported this study abroad.
